title: The U.S. and China Are Not In An A.I. Race | Interesting Times with Ross Douthat
summary: A China technology analyst argues that Beijing is pursuing AI applications and diffusion rather than racing for AGI, and that the US should step back from an all-out race framing while guarding against cyber and bio risks.

assertions.quote: I think at this point what we should do is take a step back from this all-out race framework.
China is running a different kind of race. I would argue they're running multiple races.

verdicts.note: Beijing's intentions are not public; its stated priorities stress applications and diffusion, but a covert programme cannot be ruled out.

assertions.quote: taking over TSMC would be a move too late because the chips are already made and installed

verdicts.note: A statement about Chinese leaders' intentions that no public record can show.

assertions.quote: that race mentality is driving a kind of recklessness, I would argue, from the American side.

verdicts.note: A judgement about policy motives and framing.

The 2026 Doomsday Clock statement records that the Trump administration revoked the earlier AI-safety executive order, 'a dangerous prioritization of innovation over safety', while the US, Russia and China build AI into defence; the dropped guardrail is documented, the race motive is the Board's framing.

SIPRI says fear of being left behind pushes states to integrate AI further, citing the US withdrawal in 2025 of newly introduced AI restrictions over competitiveness with China; the rescinded rule was an export framework, so this only partly fits 'safety guardrails'.
WEF says the race among major powers to integrate military AI incentivizes rapid deployment over rigorous safety testing; it describes all major powers, not the US specifically.

CNAS argues competitive pressure could lead states to shortcut testing of military AI, a 'race to the bottom' on safety, citing analogous pressures in self-driving cars and airliner autopilots; a hypothesized dynamic, not a measured US policy change.
The Bulletin says the US administration, rushing to apply AI, revoked the previous executive order on AI safety, a prioritization of AI innovation over safety that is mirrored in other major powers.

assertions.quote: the consensus is Chinese models are somewhere between 3, 6 to 9 months

verdicts.note: Benchmark trackers such as Epoch AI and Artificial Analysis estimate the gap at months rather than years.

assertions.quote: In the near term, it will slow down their AI development. In the longer term, it could speed up

verdicts.note: Controls have limited China's access to top chips while Beijing has poured money into domestic alternatives such as Huawei's Ascend.

assertions.quote: what I don't think has been overblown, in fact, maybe even underestimated up until recently is the cyber risk and the biosecurity risk

verdicts.note: AI labs and government evaluators report growing cyber-offence and bio-uplift capabilities in frontier models, though real-world harm so far is limited.

The Bulletin names the potential for AI-aided design of new pathogens as a growing biological threat, supporting the bioweapons half of the claim as an expert concern but saying nothing about cyberattacks.
Estonia's intelligence service says AI-generated code has evaded antivirus tools and AI is now used at every stage of cyberattacks; it says nothing about bioweapons.
WEF says advanced AI tools could let even small groups design bioweapons or attack infrastructure, accelerating novel weapons faster than governance adapts; a risk assessment, not measured uplift.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue that AI's dual-use nature amplifies bioterrorism and cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, where attackers hold a strong advantage; an argument without uplift data.

73% of surveyed AI researchers rated 'AI letting dangerous groups make powerful tools (e.g. engineered viruses)' a substantial or extreme concern over 30 years, but the authors say concern may reflect severity rather than likelihood.
The Bulletin reports researchers' concern that AI will be used to design new pathogens but lists cybersecurity only as a defence application, so it supports the bioweapons half only, as a concern.

assertions.quote: I would be very hesitant, certainly at this stage, to even think about binding constraints, verification agreements, a kind of arms control treaty for AI

verdicts.note: Low trust and the difficulty of verifying software make binding AI limits unlikely now; talks so far are limited to dialogue.
SIPRI judges a dedicated forum for AI-nuclear governance unrealistic given poor relations, lack of trust and asymmetric capabilities, and expects blanket prohibitions to be unlikely.
Most RAND workshop participants doubted that arms control on AI itself was feasible or desirable, many calling it a practical impossibility.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue a moratorium treaty would be toothless without verification because militaries want the hazardous capabilities and each side fears the other's secret work; an argument, not a record of failed talks.
WEF judges that the pace of innovation makes it unlikely sufficient international norms or verification mechanisms for military AI will be established in time.

The furthest the 2024 Biden-Xi talks went on military AI was a leaders' affirmation of human control over nuclear use and a call to develop military AI prudently, not a treaty; consistent with a treaty not being within reach, but the readout does not say one is infeasible.
